title: Thermal-frequency interference and scaling behavior — experiment notes
content:
Goal:
To characterize how dynamic GPU frequency/thermal throttling interacts with collective throughput and pipeline/tensor parallel execution patterns in production-like workloads. We want actionable knobs (placement, pacing, kernel selection) to reduce 95/99th token latency spikes caused by frequency churn under continuous mixed workload.

Motivation / background:
- Recent customer incidents show tail latency spikes when nodes run long-lived mixed workloads (replicated inference + background batch jobs). Suspect that changing GPU clocks (due to thermal conditions or power capping) causes NCCL schedule reshaping and temporary link congestion.
- Existing experiments in the repo focus on NCCL microbursts and packetization; this doc isolates the frequency/thermal dimension and how it amplifies or attenuates pipeline/tensor-parallel interference.

Testbed summary:
- Machines: 4x A100-80GB (2 NVLink groups: GPUs 0-1 local, 2-3 local), PCIe host staging enabled in one rack.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, NVIDIA driver 535.104, CUDA 12.2, NCCL 2.16.5, runtime: serving-runtime/commit: b3f7c9a (PR 987 referenced above).
- Thermal controls: nvidia-smi --auto-boost-default=0 (disabled), fan manual via vendor tool to force two ambient regimes: cool (fans 55%) and constrained (fans 25%). Also scripted powercap toggles via nvidia-smi --power-limit.
- Workloads: (A) Pipeline-parallel inference (3-stage micro-model approximate to Llama-7B per-stage ~3.5GB activation) with steady QPS 20; (B) Tensor-parallel replicated 8k-token generating model at QPS 5; (C) Background asynchronous allreduce jobs simulating checkpoint aggregation (large payloads, bursty).

Experiment matrix:
- Variables: fan regime (cool/constrained), power limit (default/75%), presence of background allreduce (on/off), pipeline chunking (coarse/fine), NCCL_P2P_LEVEL set to [nvlink, system], NCCL_ASYNC_PROGRESS=1 vs 0.
- Metrics collected: per-GPU SM utilization, clock charts (sm, mem, graphics), NVLink retransmit counts, PCIe read/write stalls, NCCL op latency histogram (p50/p95/p99), token-generation tail latencies, kernel-level timelines (Nsight Systems traces), and host-side enqueue/backpressure metrics from runtime.

Key observations (summary):
1) Frequency transitions correlate tightly with short-lived (50-200ms) increases in NCCL allreduce latency and NVLink retransmits. On constrained fan runs, GPUs dropped GPU-clocks by ~12% intermittently leading to 2–3x spike in collective duration.
2) Pipeline-parallel stage alignment matters: when stage boundaries and allreduce windows align, we saw constructive interference: collective starts at same time as a stage barrier -> queueing on NVLink. Staggering stage starts by 8–12ms smooths tail significantly.
3) Fine-grained pipeline chunking (smaller micro-batches) reduced host-side stall sensitivity to frequency dips; however it increased host enqueue overhead and raised baseline CPU load. Net: tail improved for token-latency-sensitive workloads but throughput dropped ~6%.
4) NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=nvlink reduced PCIe fallback but amplified per-link congestion when clocks shifted — system-level (allowing PCIe fallback) had more stable 95th tail due to opportunistic host staging.
5) Enabling NCCL_ASYNC_PROGRESS helped in scenarios where CPU had spare cycles; it reduced per-collective tail by ~15% in cool regime but provided inconsistent benefit when frequencies were oscillating because background progress interacts poorly with our runtime backpressure heuristics.

Representative run (constrained fans, power-limit=75%, background allreduce ON):
- Baseline token p99: 1140ms -> during thermal events spikes to 1860ms (observed at 2026-01-09 03:12 GMT in test logs).
- NVLink retransmits increased by 4–6x in 20–40ms window surrounding frequency descent. Nsight timeline shows TX queue saturation lasting ~30–70ms.
- Staggering pipeline stage starts by 10ms reduced observed p99 to 1220ms in identical conditions.

Instrumentation notes (how we measured):
- GPU clocks sampled via nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks.sm,clocks.mem,temperature.gpu --loop-ms=10 redirected to histograms.
- NCCL op timings via NCCL_Tests++ modified to emit per-call timestamps, aggregated with runtime traces.
- NVLink retransmits gathered from nvidia-smi --query-gpu=pcie.replay_counter (where supported) and vendor-specific nvlink counters.
- Nsight Systems light traces (30s windows) around detected tail events, saved as .qdrep (linked artifacts include PR adding auto-capture trigger).

Micro-adjustments that helped in experiments:
- Small stage staggering by 6–12ms: trivial to implement in serving-runtime scheduler as jitter per-request stage offset. Low cost, large benefit for aligned workloads.
- Adaptive chunking policy: add conservative fallback to larger chunk size when sustained frequency drops occur for >500ms to keep throughput stable. This reduced worst-case amplification of NCCL queues.
- Prefer system-level P2P when host CPU available and PCIe bandwidth headroom exists; allow policy to switch dynamically if retransmit rates exceed threshold.
- Expose a runtime knob to delay background allreduce windows during detected collective congestion windows (we can shim that into the background job controller).

Negative results / surprising failures:
- Power-limiting GPUs to avoid thermal oscillation improved some tails but introduced sustained lower throughput (expected) and in some cases caused worse fairness across replicas (hot-swap of clocks created imbalance across GPUs in same node).
- Offloading to PCIe (NCCL system) in some cases created longer sustained tail because PCIe read amplification and host staging caused persistent queueing; in other cases it reduced instant spikes — tradeoff depends on workload shape.

Open questions / next experiments:
1) Test at larger scales (8+ GPUs across 2 nodes) with mixed topologies (NVLink mesh + NVSwitch) — does NVSwitch topology mask frequency-induced retransmits?
2) Controlled thermal gradients across card set: if some GPUs are hotter (simulating heterogeneous workload placement) does imbalance create persistent NCCL imbalance?
3) Evaluate combining our adaptive staging cache (prefix KV) to decrease cross-node collective size during thermal events; measure quality vs token-cost tradeoffs.
4) Longer-term: can we feed thermal predictions (from sensors) into the scheduler for proactive stage staggering?

Runbook suggestions (short-term ops):
- If on-call sees recurring p99 spikes during mixed workloads, query GPU clocks and NVLink retransmit counters; if retransmits spike concurrently with clocks descending, temporarily enable stage staggering and increase chunking granularity.
- Add an alert on sustained retransmit-rate > X for 30s aggregated across node; tie alert to automatic temporary throttling of background-allreduce windows.

Implementation tasks (rough):
- [P1] Add per-request stage-start jitter (6–12ms) toggleable via route config. (est 2d) — owner: Arjun
- [P1] Instrumentation: add per-collective retransmit metrics into telemetry and surface them in console. (est 3d) — owner: Maya
- [P2] Adaptive chunking heuristic: shrink/grow chunk based on recent clock stability window. (est 5d) — owner: Luis
- [P3] Background job controller: add congestion-aware pause/resume API. (est 3d) — owner: Rina

Notes to reviewers:
- PR 987 includes the lightweight capture hook and initial stage-jitter implementation; tests included in PR are synthetic. Need more realistic long-run tests (24h) before rollout.
- Please sanity-check thresholds for retransmit-rate alerting; current draft threshold is 1000 retransmits/min/node which may be noisy.

Attached artifacts / references:
- Jira: INF-2123 (incident and initial triage)
- Github PR 987 (lightweight capture + stage jitter)
- Slack thread: #runtime-perf \"thermal spikes and nvlink retransmits\" (link above)
- Nsight exports and aggregated CSVs uploaded to test-results/thermal-run-2026-01-09 (internal path)

Conclusion:
Thermal/frequency dynamics are a meaningful amplifier of existing collective/transient interference modes. Mitigations that do not require hardware changes (stage staggering, adaptive chunking, and smarter policy on P2P level) give large wins for tail latency with low implementation cost. Next step: run 48h mixed workload soak with stage-stagger enabled and telemetry on retransmits to validate stability before rolling as default for production routes that mix pipeline and replicated tensor-parallel workloads.

-- End of notes --
